title: Agreements that grew past their first ceiling
question: Which City agreements now stand above the amount first agreed, by how much, and does each look like more years of the same service or the same work costing more?
finding: Of 622 agreements with a first and a latest ceiling in the Board's files, 369 grew: from $9.09 billion to $19.04 billion together, $9.95 billion more. 305 grew by a quarter or more and 158 at least doubled. Read by their dates, 191 of the 369 are more years at about the same yearly cost, 72 are more years at a higher yearly cost, 79 are a higher ceiling for the same term, and 27 cannot be told. The largest rise in percent is APX Inc. (Public Utilities Commission, $5.0 million to $149.9 million); the largest in dollars is Mckesson Plasma And Biologics LLC (Public Health, $295.9 million to $1.47 billion). Where the first approval itself is on file, so that the agreement is followed from the start, 46 of 304 (15%) later grew by a quarter or more.
how: Board of Supervisors titles from 2014 to 2026 were linked into one record per agreement, following only links proven by a dollar figure carried from one title to the next or by a shared contract number (the rule used in the amendment-growth screen). The first amount is the total in the first approval on file or, where the first file is an amendment, the amount that amendment says it started from; the latest is the highest total approved. Left out: 527 leases and property; 225 no usable name in the title; 167 agreements with other public bodies; 164 no amount in any title; 58 loans; 21 agreements that bring money in (concessions, rents, franchises). Each row is then read from its dates: if the end date did not move, it is "same term, higher ceiling"; if it moved and the ceiling per year of term stayed within 25% of the first, "more years at about the same yearly cost"; if the yearly figure rose by more, "more years and a higher yearly cost". Dates are taken from the wording of the titles (the latest date in a title is taken as the end it now runs to; "extend by two years" gives the end before). The City's own contract table keeps only the present ceiling and end date of each contract, with no first amount, so it cannot be used for this; 49 further Board agreements are left out because no title states what the first amount was. The table lists all measured increases, ordered by percentage change and then by the latest ceiling.
limits: Each step here was approved in a public vote. Most of these are services the City chose to keep buying: a shelter, a treatment programme, a software licence or a security contract extended for more years at much the same yearly cost is a renewal, not an overrun, and the row says so where the dates allow. A ceiling is the most that may be spent, not what was spent; an as-needed or master agreement has a ceiling that is a limit on orders. Only agreements that needed a Board vote appear (under Charter section 9.118, broadly a contract of $10 million or more and a later amendment of more than $500,000 to one), so smaller contracts are absent, and so is nearly all construction, which departments and their commissions award and change under their own authority. Titles are text-mined: an amount or date can be misread, and each row links to its file. Pandemic emergency work explains several of the steepest rises in 2020 and 2021. An agreement first seen at an amendment is in the files because it grew, so the share that grew among all rows overstates the true rate; the rate among agreements followed from their first approval is the fair one. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
